utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. We can hear you well. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. All right. Mr. Hodzic, over to you. Perhaps you can inform us whether or not you will be able to proceed with the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear any translation. PRESIDING OFFICER: Can you hear me now, the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I hear it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Good morning. I was asking [Microphone not activated] what your decision was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Featherstone, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: I was inquiring what your decision is as regards cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having followed the examination of this witness carefully over the past two days, the examination carried out by my learned friend of the Prosecution, and also having familiarised myself with the interview of the witness and other documents, I deem it necessary nevertheless to put some questions to Mr. Karic in order to have justice served and in order to establish the facts involved. So I am prepared to cross-examine. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. In that case, Mr. Hodzic, if you'd like to proceed with your cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Hodzic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, I'm Ahmet Hodzic, attorney at law, and I've been on this case of Mr. Sefer Halilovic since recently. Could you please answer some questions I have for you, and all of it with a view to clarifying certain facts pertaining to the evidence that you gave over the past two days, as well as what you said during your interview previously. My first question would be the following: The interview and the statement you gave over the past two days show that you were present on the 21st and on the 22nd in Zenica, is that correct, and that you attended the meeting there?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, although -- I'm sorry. I am really sorry. I would like to ask you, although you have already told us certain things, could you tell us, at least briefly, about the contents of that particular meeting held there.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was considered necessary for the General Staff, along with the majority of corps commanders and members of the Main Staff, headed by Rasim Delic, have a meeting, a military meeting, which would deal with various organisational, personnel, logistic, and other weaknesses that had been displayed until then. That was indeed done. During those two days, we analysed the entire situation in the war theatre in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Finally, conclusions were adopted that were binding on all corps commanders, especially the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, except for Dudakovic, who was not present. That was the commander of the 4th Corps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the 5th Corps. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also the 6th Corps commander was involved. Tasks were given, assignments were given, and it became obvious that the situation was particularly dramatic in the area of the 4th Corps, namely, the area of Mostar. It was threatened, and the overall situation there was one of danger coming from the HVO, especially Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps, referred to this. It was said several times what the situation was like, and he asked for specific assistance several times. After the two-day meeting, the commanders adopted some resolutions, some conclusions, and it was said that the Main Staff should assist the 4th Corps as early as possible. NERETVA-93 was not referred to at all. That followed later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the previous question, I put it to you, in order to reiterate once again: Does this mean that at this meeting there was no reference whatsoever made to NERETVA-93?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it means. It was said, and it was concluded, that Herzegovina and Mostar should be assisted, specifically the 4th Corps, but the Operation NERETVA-93 was not referred to specifically at all. That ensued later.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause before putting the next question. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic and Mr. Karic, you have the benefit of communicating in the same language. Please remember that this does all have to be interpreted for the rest of us to follow. So if you leave a break before -- when one of you has finished before the next starts, that would be appreciated by all of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I shall pay attention to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us your position on the following: When was the definite decision passed to establish a team that was supposed to help the 4th and 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have before me my notebook, in which it says that this -- follow the contacts that were had and everything that was done by the Main Staff. So this was the second half of August 1993. That is when this idea was conceived, that the Main Staff, through establishing an inspection team, could effect the actual developments in Herzegovina, which followed towards the end of August. An order was issued to establish this inspection team, headed by Sefer Halilovic, chief of the Main Staff, and that team was supposed to be sent off to Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this order read?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It read as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karic please slow down for the interpreters. We do not have a copy.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dated the 30th of August, 1993, on the establishment of an inspection team, in order to coordinate combat activities, as well as all other duties and tasks in the area of responsibility of the 3rd, 4th, and 6th Corps. And then Halilovic, Suljevic, Bilajac, Karic, Najetovic, Dzankovic, those were the members. The team went on the 28th of August 1993 to carry out the mentioned order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the numbers at the outset, the preamble, so to speak. PRESIDING OFFICER: Indeed. And I believe this would be the witness's diary that was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: No. It's obviously not the witness's diary. The witness is referring to a specific order and he was asked by Defence counsel to read out the order. The witness is requested to read out the order in full, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: Let me just have a word with the registrar and see what we can do about this technically. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like to request the technician in Sarajevo to put the camera on the document, please, so the people here can follow it on their video evidence screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the following: What I have in front of me is not the complete order, the original order from that period. What I have here is a copy of our report, where we invoked the order that I quoted a few minutes ago at the very beginning. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So this is the report of the inspection team that was addressed to the General Staff and all of those present signed it at the end. However, what is mentioned, what is mentioned, is that on the basis of such-and-such an order, dated such-and-such a date, number such-and-such, we carried out this assignment and we are submitting our report. So you should not that I this is the original order that I have in front of me with the entire text. I haven't got that order. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, thank you. We understand that. Could you just for the record, though, set out what is the date and title of the document you have in front of you, and then Mr. Hodzic, do you have a copy of that here? You do have a copy of that? Right. Then in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the distinguished Prosecutor the following: I think that he has a copy in English. This is their document. It would not be a bad thing for the Presiding Officer to have the English version before her when this is discussed. I have a copy in the Bosnian language, but unfortunately I don't have a copy in the English language, and in this way, things would be faster and easier. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. But if you're going to be putting documents to the witness, it obviously helps if we know in advance and can have copies available in the courtroom. Mr. Withopf, is this a document that's been disclosed by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document Defence is referring to. We haven't been informed prior to this session -- documents will be used by the Defence. I'm not in a position to judge on it. The document I see on the screen is in Bosnian language. I'm not in a position to say whether we have such a document or whether we have it not. Defence counsel is kindly asked to provide to the Prosecution prior to cross-examining the witness the documents he wishes to use as did Prosecution prior to the examination-in-chief of the witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic, do you have other documents that you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just have this one single document that I wish to put to the witness. I do apologise for having made this error in procedure. PRESIDING OFFICER: Well, if it's only the one document, I'm sure we can manage to resolve this. First of all, if the court deputy in Sarajevo could make sure that a copy is obtained of what is actually before the witness in Sarajevo. I think we should also mark it for identification, subject, of course, to English -- well, a working language translation being produced as well. Mr. Hodzic, you have a copy there. For the record, could you read out exactly what is the title and the date of the document so that we have a proper description for the record. And then, unless Mr. Withopf has anything more he'd like to point out, we can continue with the line of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say the following: This document that is on the screen is not one that I had mentioned at all, and I don't have a copy of it. The document I have is one that I'm going to read out very carefully. It's not very long and I'll read it in its entirety. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. Well, as the witness has a different document in front of him, that needs -- the document that he has needs to be marked for identification. Otherwise we will be in a terrible muddle. Then the document you have, I understand, is a different document, which should also be marked. Is it possible for us to put that -- well, the difficulty is for the witness in Sarajevo to see and to follow the document that you have, Mr. Hodzic. Again, I'll be guided by the registry. Is there some way we can show that document to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. Right. The registrar will mark the document in Sarajevo. It is then possible, I understand, for this to be -- the document to be placed on the ELMO so that everyone can see it. You just have the one copy, Mr. Hodzic, or you have a spare that you can refer to while one goes on the ELMO? Right. Sorry about the confusion, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document referred to by the witness will be marked for identification IMF D1. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, you can see that document now on the screen, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. And are the interpreters able to see a copy in some form and follow? Excellent. Right. Then, Mr. Hodzic, if you'd like to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's what the heading says. "The staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo," number, illegible. "Date, 30th August 1993." On the right-hand side it says: "The defence of the Republic, military secret, strictly confidential. Contents: In accordance with --" PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, Mr. Withopf. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects that Defence counsel translates the document. If he hasn't any official translation available, therefore he can't use it. He is not -- doesn't have the capacity to translate it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Is it not being translated by our interpreters at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's probably my understanding, yes. I apologise. It was a misunderstanding. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. Okay. Please continue, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading it. I'm not translating it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Indeed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start from the very beginning as for the contents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they cannot see it on the ELMO any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In accordance with the conclusions reached at the meeting of the Main Staff and the corps commanders, and in order to redress current omissions and weaknesses in the areas of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps, I hereby order, number 1, to establish an expert team-inspection with a view to coordinating tasks and assignments in the areas of responsibility of the 4th and 6th Corps. The basic tasks of the team shall be as follows: Viewing B/G," which means combat readiness, "of the commands and units, specifically in the field, and commanding and controlling combat operations." A new item now: "Assessment of the possibilities of the forces and resources, and the use of the aforementioned in accordance with that." New item: "Resolving personnel matters and logistic support in all segments." Again a new item: "The functioning of the civilian authorities and adapting it to the needs of the armed struggle and the liberation war." Number 2: "I hereby appoint as team leader the chief of the General Staff of the armed forces, Sefer Halilovic, and I appoint the following persons as members of the team within the General Staff of the armed forces, namely, number 1, Suljevic Zicro, Suljevic Zicro. Number 2, Bilajac Rifat. Number 3, Vehbija Karic. Number 4, Dzemal Najetovic. Number 5, Edin Hasanspahic, and number 6, Namik Dzankovic." Number 3: "The chief of staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces shall, in accordance with his powers, resolve on site, through his own orders" -- I'm sorry. It's hard to read -- "and he shall inform me about this regularly. And in case there are radical measures" -- I beg Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your pardon. It is very illegible. "And in case there are some more radical proposals made, or solutions to that effect, he should consult me -- he should certainly consult me." Number 4: "The control should start on the 31st of August. There's -- "and it should be finished by" -- and then there's no date -- "1993. Upon return, file a report in writing. And as for important matters during the inspection itself, reports should be submitted verbally." On the left-hand side, "ADZ/IH." On the right-hand side, "commander of the staff -- staff of the Supreme Command, Rasim Delic," and his signature follows. And there's a number too, but that number was the one assigned by the Prosecution. So that is the substance of this document. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Do you have some -- well, perhaps before moving on to any particular questions you have of the witness on that, we should just deal with the practicalities. It does bear a number which appears to show that it has come from the Prosecution. So the Prosecution are aware of the document, but I assume were not aware that it was going to be put to this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are aware of this document. We were not told the Defence would use it today. However, we have the document in front of us. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Do you have any objection to its admission for the purposes of the deposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We don't have any objection. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. Then, Madam Registrar can give it a number for the purposes of the deposition. Thank you. I think if there's no objection to it, it can be given a number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked VK D1. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Hodzic. Please continue. Sorry. It's been a long process to get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the Presiding Officer something. I have certain personal problems. I was wounded in the course of the war. I sustained a wound to the leg, and it's very difficult for me to remain standing. Would it be at all possible for me to sit down? PRESIDING OFFICER: Of course you may, Mr. Hodzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Featherstone, please. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes, of course, Mr. Hodzic. Please do. Just do make sure you have your microphone on when you're speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, I would like to ask you to explain to us how this team understood this order with regard to items 1 to 4. Could you explain each item individually, please.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could say that the team took this in a very professional sense. They took this order from the commander of the Main Staff very seriously, and they strictly adhered to this order, which is the result of our responsibility, our military background, military education that we had in the pre-war period, and also a result of the positions that we held in the BH army. Orders were professionally carried out. The order was professionally carried out, the order from the commander of the supreme staff of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain individual items mentioned in this order so that the Presiding Officer might be in a position to see what its substance is. Under item 1, examining combat readiness, what does this mean?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that we should take a realistic view, an objective view of the situation, in the units of the 4th, 6th, and 3rd Corps that have been mentioned, and the focus is on the 4th and the 6th Corps, which were located in Herzegovina, and whose zone of responsibility was in Herzegovina. It was necessary to review the strength of the unit's logistics support, the ammunition situation, the situation with regard to discipline, morale, the experience in combat activity to date, all of those most important issues were to be reviewed, the most important issues which influenced the combat readiness of the units mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here it also says commanding and controlling combat activity. How did you take this? What does this mean for you, commanding and controlling this? Does this refer to the commander of units in the field who were commanding and controlling combat activities or was something else at stake?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that we understood it in the following way: The substance of the order was that we didn't have a commanding function and subordinate commanders were aware of this fact, but we certainly had an influence on having the order obeyed when preparing for the Operation NERETVA-93 and all other issues. On all other issues we exercised our authority to influence other issues in accordance with the order from the commander of the supreme staff, and decisions were taken on the level of the operation centre of the Main Staff, and at the level of corps commands. Decisions on how to use units, et cetera. We coordinated, cooperated, in order to ensure that all the tasks that had been assigned were implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your suggestions, your proposals, and your opinions, were the commanders of the units who were in that area at the time obliged to obey them?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were not in a position to take decisions in the sense of issuing orders, since we didn't have such a function, but nevertheless, through daily contact with commanders in the field, in such contacts they showed respect for our suggestions, our requests, et cetera. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic, please may I remind you to allow time for the interpretation to finish. Thank you. If you can perhaps -- you hear the English through your headsets, but you're starting to cut off the end of the witness's response. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: I think the witness has finished his response to your question, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a professional military organ, when assisting and compiling certain documents, did you encounter certain situations in which the commander --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the officer concerned --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Hodzic please repeat the initial question. It wasn't quite clear.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain -- at certain moments, because we lacked the authority, we weren't in a position to orders, since our function was to carry out inspections and review the combat readiness of the units in the field and to review how combat activity was being controlled, we saw that our influence had been diminished and people were avoiding meeting members of the inspection team. There was the commander of the 6th Corps, Salko Gusic, so that Sefer Halilovic himself, over a period of several days, insisted on meeting him, but this man avoided such a meeting. And this was one of the indicators. It showed that we were encountering obstructions and that there was no respect for the chief of staff or for us, as a professional inspection team. The second case was the failure to implement the order of the commander of the Prozor Battalion, Enver Buza, when he was 24 hours late in bringing in the battalion, and he justified this by saying that he didn't have sufficient fuel. I am not sure whether he obeyed the orders of his corps, Salko Gusic, the orders of the commander of his corps, Salko Gusic. I assume that he may have said that that is how he should act. But I can't claim this for a fact. And also the supply of logistics and ammunition from Konjic, which was obviously part of the preparation for the operation. This supply encountered many difficulties. Vehicles got bogged down in certain stream, there are no other possibilities for sending other vehicles. But we could see that logistics supplies had been obstructed, and I can't say where this came from. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic, I'm very sorry, but you're again cutting off the end of the witness, and it's not helping us to understand what's going on. So please, you can either see it on the transcript when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the -- when that stops moving on the screen, or perhaps by just having one ear tuned to the English channel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, or someone from your team, issue an order for combat orders, and was the order simply shredded by the person who received it?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. That was Zulfikar Alispago. We submitted an order to him for the forthcoming combat activities, with a working map and a decision. Later on we found out that when he returned to his command post in Donja Jablanica, he tore that order of ours and that working map with the decision. He tore it up. He wrote an order of his own. The defence of national rights, Vrnik [phoen] 93. None of us had authorised him to do that. But you could feel his willfulness, his reluctance to accept decisions, and the role of his units, and the specific military tasks in the forthcoming operation. So Zulfikar Alispago, the commander of special units in Donja Grabovica, did this. I apologise. In Donja Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of role did Alispago have in this operation, in the operation for raising the blockade of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His unit had been in that area from earlier on. It was a local one there, and its task was to use rafts and boats to cross part of the lake below the hydroelectric power station in Grabovica, and he was to use his units to reconnoitre and carry out sabotage activities in the direction of Vrde. Later on, it turned out that he was successful in crossing the Jablanica lake, and in using those units, but after the operation had been ongoing for a few days - and we have such information - after a few days, he spoke with the imam from the Zagreb mosque, who had arrived in Jablanica, Sefko Omerbasic. That was the name of the imam. And so in order to prevent him using the units and combat action, he gave him 50.000 marks, and soon afterwards you could feel that he was obstructing the use of his units in combat activity along that axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the units of Zulfikar Alispago, and who commanded those units?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfikar Alispago, also known as Zuka, with Nihad Bojadzic, who was his assistant and deputy, commanded that unit, and throughout that period, he -- Zulfikar Alispago, Zuka, was in command of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the inspection team, to be more specific, Sefer Halilovic, as the chief of the team, was he in a position to command those units and to issue binding orders to them?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the field, most of the commanders accepted and respected us, most of the commanders in most of the units accepted us, because they knew us from before as people, as officers, and this was also because of the functions that we held at that period. The difficulties that were encountered by the commander of the 6th Corps, and the difficulties encountered in the case of Zulfikar Alispago and Enver Buza, these difficulties show that the behaviour was not professional. It was not responsible with respect to our role. We were trying to implement Operation 93 and we were trying to meet people, direct them, and issue specific assignments with regard to that operation, to the extent that we had the authority to do so, according to the order of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in this order dated the 30th of August, 1993, when the inspection team was formed, there is not a single item in which the team, or rather, Sefer Halilovic, is given the authority to command the units that are in that area?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that. I agree with that, because in none of the items in the order that we are discussing, in none of those items is Sefer or someone from the team given such a role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this order has been supplemented by some other order which might have conferred such authority on the inspection team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no other order, apart from the arrival, the personal arrival of the commander of the Main Staff, temporary command post in Donja Jablanica, to be more specific, in the command of Zulfikar Alispago. The commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic, together with his associates, Sulejman Vrana, Alija Loncaric. On the 4th of September, in the afternoon, the 4th of September, 1993. He was briefed, or, to be more specific, the Chief of Staff, Sefer Halilovic, briefed him. He signed a combat orders and documents, decisions, about the operation, in accordance with military reason, he took over command responsibility for the entire operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the term "Operation NERETVA-93" used for the first time?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I can't remember the exact date, but I think that it was when we arrived in Herzegovina, during that period, and when we started preparations to assist Mostar. I think that is when the term "NERETVA-93" and the operation to help Mostar was first used. So that would be at the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the documents in which this operation was planned and which contains a certain map, and the directions of action for individual units is also marked there, in those documents, was there a decision as to who would be in command of that operation?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I participated with Rifat Bilajac and Zicro Suljevic and Sefer. We all worked on these documents for the plan of action and we all worked on the working map, and this was certified by the commander of the supreme staff. As I said, on the 4th of September, in Donja Jablanica. PRESIDING OFFICER: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but Mr. Withopf, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I have an objection to this question. Defence may please produce the documents Defence counsel is referring to and the witness is going to explain. PRESIDING OFFICER: You mean the map and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Exactly. The map and the other documents that are referred to. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic, do you have the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, and I'll withdraw this question. I'll ask another question. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other document in which the commander of the Operation 93 was designated?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was no other document, and Sefer was selected and mentioned in the decision and the working map as the commander of that operation, as the most senior member of the team at that moment in time. Rasim accepted this and he considered it to be quite normal. He signed a document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't understood you completely. I'll repeat my question. Is there any other document, any other order, in which someone was appointed, someone was designated, to command the Operation NERETVA-93, which was given that name at the time?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were no additional orders, no additional orders in which an individual was designated as the commander of Operation NERETVA-93. We took it for granted that this should be the most senior member of the team, and the documents that were compiled were compiled in this sense. And such documents were authenticated and certified by Rasim Delic, the commander of the Main Staff, on the 4th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the term "team." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that when we left Sarajevo, on the basis of the order authorising us to leave Sarajevo, on the basis of that order, we were not in a position to think about the command role that we might be exercising when carrying out that task, which was thrust upon us when we went to Herzegovina. And we took it for granted that the coordination, the direction of the activity of the operation should be carried out by one person. That was the commander of the General Staff, Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in command of combat activity of the units that were acting along a certain axis?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commanders and the brigade commanders, who were in command, on the basis of the orders of their superiors. And coordination and direction, influencing the effectiveness of the units in the course of combat activity, this was Sefer's role. Sefer was the most senior officer in our team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that situation, was Sefer Halilovic authorised to command and issue orders to individual commanders? I mean, was he in a position to issue binding orders?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation was such that he had to be in a position to influence the commanders, to make them issue certain orders, but in accordance with the main order, in which we were ordered to leave Sarajevo as an inspection team. And as the situation developed, and in accordance with the order mentioned, the order of the commander of the Main Staff, the situation was such that he was not in a position to remain passive. He had to issue certain orders, but this had to remain within the limits of the order issued by the commander of the supreme staff, Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the order dated the 30th of August, 1993, on the formation of the inspection team?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm referring to, the order that you read out in front of everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And another question: You're a staff officer and you have compiled a fair number of maps. You have drafted a fair number of maps. When planning a certain operation, is it necessary to also mark the appropriate, the relevant command posts on the maps?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is common practice. You also mark command posts on maps, whether it's the main command post or the forward or temporary command post. But usually it is marked on the map, and this is the case in all armies -- PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic --

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- throughout the world. PRESIDING OFFICER: [Previous translation continues]... onto a new area of questioning, do you have a few more questions along this line that you'd like to finish now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're quite right. I would like to move on to another field, another area, and I agree that we should have a break now. PRESIDING OFFICER: Fine. Then we'll adjourn for 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Just before we continue, Mr. Hodzic, I wonder if you might be able to give us -- I wonder if you might be able to give us any indication of how long you're likely to be with the witness. I understand for practical reasons it would be helpful to know if we're likely to go into tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today will be sufficient. I will manage to finish my questions today. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. And of course it may be that the Prosecution has some re-examination. But thank you for that guidance. If you'd like to continue with your questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, as for the map that refers to NERETVA-93, was there a command post marked on it?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer with any certainty. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, before you respond to that, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I object to this question. Defence counsel may please produce the map he's referring to. PRESIDING OFFICER: I think Mr. Hodzic has already responded that he does not have that map. It is the same map, Mr. Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same map. I haven't got it, so I withdraw this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, when did the Operation NERETVA-93 start? When did the combat operations actually start?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preparations started in the beginning of September 1993, and specifically, combat operations started, and I'll tell you now after I've referred to my logbook, I'll tell you when they started. I think combat operations started on Monday, the 13th of September, 1993, in the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next question: The commanders who commanded the units in this operation, who did they report to with regard to these combat operations and the results achieved?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as expected, and as customary, they submitted reports to their corps command, and in their contacts with us too. There were some briefings, short ones, and also they briefed Sefer Halilovic when he toured certain command posts during his activities, like in Buturovic Polje, the 45th Brigade. But for the most part, the official channels were to the superior commands, that is to say, the corps commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades, who commanded these two brigades in the NERETVA-93 operation?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that it's a bit surprising, even given this time distance of ten years, that the commander of the 9th Brigade, Ramiz Delalic, Celo, brought his unit down there, and he relinquished the unit to the company commanders and platoon commanders, and he was engaged in activities of his own near Konjic. He was buying weapons from deserters, and he said that allegedly he was supposed to take these weapons into Sarajevo. And Caco also relinquished his command and his direct insight, I mean the troops, the company that he brought from Sarajevo, because he was engaged in certain activities in Jablanica. So it so turned out that even teachers, when taking children on a school trip, would not behave that way. They would take the children back to the parents and take them back home. But these men behaved in a non-military manner. Caco returned after a few days to Sarajevo, without asking anyone anything. I mean, this was a total irresponsibility, and this was totally out of line in terms of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, these units, had they been resubordinated to Zulfikar Alispago?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alispago?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I managed to understand what you were saying, according to this order pertaining to the establishment of the inspection team, Sefer Halilovic did not have any command authority to command units in combat operations; is that right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the order, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To command combat operations?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in accordance with the order. Not in accordance with the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the order now. And later on we'll move on to other matters.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the structure of the organisations of RBH, there was the commander of the supreme staff, there was the chief of Main Staff, and also two deputy chiefs. Please give me an answer to the following: In this chain of command, and when there is singleness of command, who commanded the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was I clear?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite clear. I find you quite clear. In this structure of the top echelons of the army, perhaps you forgot to mention that the presidency is the Supreme Command, according to the constitution in that period, that is to say, Alija Izetbegovic, as president of the presidency, together with the members of the presidency. In this organ, the Supreme Command, he was there, Sefer Halilovic was also there, ex officio, and then after that, after the 8th of June, the commander of the Main Staff, Rasim Delic; and then there was the commander, the Chief of Staff, the two deputy chiefs, and then finally the corps commands and the organs of the General Staff, with the heads of relevant departments. So that would be the top echelons of the military. Concrete decisions with regard to this operation too and this decision had to be done in coordination with the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the Supreme Command, and it was headed by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this chain of command, the Chief of Staff, was he authorised to issue orders within unit command?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since you have the order there at the Honourable Court itself, and quite unequivocally, it does not give anybody the right, Sefer Halilovic included, to act independently or to be in a command position independently. The order is quite unequivocal in terms of our powers and also the powers of Sefer Halilovic, although he was Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the commander transfer command authority to the commander or the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he could, and this is very frequent practice within the military. But he did not do that. He approved the plan of action and all documents for this action, and he verified this by a signature, and they were in communication regarding particular subject-matters. So not through a single order and not through a single gesture did he put himself in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. One question: During your examination, you said the following, that they had said to you, or rather, that you had heard that Celo had come to Jablanica, and Caco had also come to Jablanica, with his soldiers. One question: At that time, did you see Caco, Celo, and their soldiers? Did you see that they had actually arrived in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but as I was returning from a particular assignment that had to do with contacts with the municipal staff, I saw Adnan Solakovic. He was taking a rest, and this was near the office building of the hydroelectric power plant in Jablanica. We had a meeting with the authorities from Jablanica there, and during the meeting, Bakir Alispahic came in. He was Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. And he offered us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and he told us -- he told all of us who were present there that Alija Izetbegovic, as supreme commander, as a member of the Supreme Command, gives full support to the forthcoming operation, and he wished us luck in terms of succeeding in this. So I did not go out. I did not see Celo and Caco, but I had heard, I had heard that they had arrived too. PRESIDING OFFICER: Just a minute, Mr. Hodzic. There was some confusion in the middle of the interpretation of Mr. Karic's answer. Mr. Karic, you responded that there was a meeting and Bakir Alispahic came in. He was the Minister of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and he offered -- and then we lost the rest of that. Could you just repeat for the record, if you recall, what it was that you were trying to say at that stage. Thank you. And while I have the microphone, Mr. Hodzic, I must remind you once more, please, to allow a little more time for the interpreters to finish the answer to the questions. Thank you. Mr. Karic, if you can clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can repeat what I said. During the mentioned meeting with the authorities and the commanders of the local brigades, the 44th Brigade from Jablanica, Enes Kovacevic, we had a meeting on the premises there, that is, at the office building of the hydroelectric power plant Jablanica. Bakir Alispahic appeared during the meeting. We all said hello, and he conveyed the following: "I've come to see you. The Supreme Commander, President Izetbegovic, sends his regards to you. He is giving you his moral support, wishing you success in the operation, and I have brought you 50 members of the Lasta Detachment to help you in the operation." We accepted that, and the same night he went to Mostar via Mount Prenj, and he took the Lastas with him. And we found it strange the next day, because we had given the assignment to Enes Kovacevic to put them up and deploy them the next day, according to the existing plan of operation. So nothing came out of it, in actual fact. During this meeting, I found out that Caco had arrived from Sarajevo, as well as Ramiz Delalic, with their troops, and I saw, as I was entering the premises where the meeting was held, I saw Adnan Solakovic with a group of his soldiers. We greeted each other, and I let them go and find their accommodation, because Zulfikar Alispago had been given the assignment earlier on to find proper accommodation for them. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, do you know where Sefer Halilovic was between the 4th and 9th of September, 1993? In which area was he?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that Sefer, in agreement with Rasim, when he visited us on the 4th, that we all spent the night in Konjic, between the 4th and the 5th, and that Sefer, on the 5th, went to Sarajevo to intervene. So that these units would be moved, the 9th and the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes that there was a pause in the transmission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in terms of time, I cannot say where he was all the time, but I know that he was absent, and I know that with Rasim Delic's approval, he went to Sarajevo, because Rasim went on to the command of the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, when did you see him again the next time, I mean after the 5th? When did you see him again? Let me be more precise. Was this the day after the crime had been committed? Was that when you came to your premises?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at my notes now. I'm looking at my notebook, rather. This was on the 9th. It was on the 9th when he returned, a day after the crime had been committed, the crime in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you found out about this crime in Grabovica, could you please repeat to us briefly what you did then, you as the team that was in Jablanica at that time.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it is superfluous to say that we were surprised, like any normal person would be. We were taken by surprise, in terms of what had happened. So in the morning of the 9th, Namik Dzankovic informed us, he told us that in Grabovica, a crime had been committed against civilians, that they were thrown into the Neretva River, and the information that he had by then was that 19 Croats had been killed in a criminal way. In addition to being surprised, and that was our personal experience and feeling at the time, we told him, ordered him, immediately to be even more persistent in his contacts with the security organs from the 44th Brigade, with the municipal authorities, and to establish an even stronger team that would go out and deal with investigation-related issues on site. And that Zulfikar Alispago and the 44th Brigade should provide additional security and not allow anyone to leave Donja Grabovica, the area of Donja Grabovica, before all of this is taken care of and before the perpetrators of this crime are identified. Also, he was immediately supposed to draft a telegram in order to notify the security administration and Jusuf Jasarevic, his chief. And also, we told him to keep us abreast of all new information at any time, day or night. That is the essence of what we ordered him to do, and he proceeded to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, according to the order that was already mentioned, the 30th of August, 1993, did you have any more authority in terms of what you could do in this respect? Did you have any authority to initiate court proceedings or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not, because the system functioned. We were in the role that we were in, and we had had the task that we had been given, the subordination of the 6th Corps, that is their area of responsibility, and also the security administration of the Main Staff. Rasim Delic was also informed immediately, as commander. And the same day, the security administration was informed. It sent a certain number of people to reinforce the investigation, and it was -- the matter was being resolved on the basis of the system, because the security administration and the security organs in Sarajevo, as far as I know, directly, and later, as far as I know, in terms of what happened in October and November, when everybody was arrested, they got quite accurate information about the perpetrators of the crime, that is to say, they had their actual names and surnames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, as a high-ranking officer of the JNA for many years, did you know who in the army of the former JNA - and also this was taken over by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina later - what authorities were involved in investigating the crimes perpetrated by military personnel? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it is military organs primarily, military security organs, that were involved in the matter now as well, but in this specific situation they were being assisted by the municipal authorities of security from the MUP, and also the security authorities from the 44th local Jablanica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After establishing the perpetrators of the crime, whose duty was it to start further proceedings, and who was in charge of asking for an investigation to be instituted subsequently?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military structure, was the security administration that was in charge of collecting all this information and then handing them over to the military prosecutor, and then the perpetrators were brought into custody by the court. Some of the protagonists were actually sentenced. But somebody from the military leadership - and I cannot say who, but it can be assumed who could have reached a decision from the absolute top of the state to have them released. So they were released. They managed to get hold of passports and a vast majority are abroad nowadays, from Canada to Australia, and they are out of reach of the justice authorities and of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Karic, that the inspection team did not have any authority in terms of discovering who the perpetrators are and then filing criminal reports and also initiating procedure by military judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The team had nothing to do with this. We had been marginalised, since, on the 26th of October, the Chief of Staff was arrested, and all of us who were on the inspection team were marginalised because of that. So this was indeed felt. We were simply sidetracked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said now that on the 26th of October, the perpetrators of the crime in Grabovica were known by then and that Sefer Halilovic was also taken into custody then. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That is when the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was brought into custody, detained, and an investigation -- this investigation went on for a month, and afterwards he was sent to his family, home. And until the end of the war, he had no rights whatsoever. He did not even receive humanitarian aid that veterans were entitled to, and also he did not have an official vehicle. He was quite marginalised. And he was deprived of all of his rights, the constitutional rights of any citizen, something that he had voluntarily opted for. So this was an injustice, injustice from the point of view of personnel and from the point of view of morality itself. This was done vis-a-vis Sefer Halilovic. I personally opposed that at the time, and I also had to bear the consequences of that, because those who belonged to the system called me one of Sefer's men. I visited him and I thought that a man should not be abandoned altogether, regardless of whether he had made a mistake or the extent to which he had made a mistake. However, he should not be reject altogether, because in the combat operations until then, during the war, he had given a great deal to the defence of the country and the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, does this mean that from the 26th onwards, when they found out about the perpetrators of the crime, Sefer Halilovic no longer had any influence within the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. A day or two later I visited him. There was security in front of his office. He wasn't even allowed to use -- he wasn't even allowed to use the communication system or anything else. He was under house arrest. He had no freedom to carry out any of his human needs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, in the course of the evidence you presented yesterday, and this is something that you have previously stated too, you said that when the crime in Grabovica came to light, you said that this was perpetrated by units of the 9th and 10th Motorised Brigade. My question is as follows: When this crime in Grabovica came to light, was it -- did people know who the perpetrators of the crimes were, or were these just pure assumptions?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, and right up until our return to Sarajevo, and up until the investigation, towards the end of October 1993, we didn't know the individual names of the perpetrators of the crime in Grabovica, but we did know that they were members of those two units. From the very beginning, we knew this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal knowledge of this or was it a matter of assumptions? What was the basis for this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was on the basis of the information that we got from Namik Dzankovic, according to which a crime had been committed in Grabovica, and according to his initial information that he obtained 24 hours later, the crime was committed by members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this conclusion reached on the basis of the fact that the units of the 9th and 10th Brigade were at that location, or is there any firmer evidence on the basis of which such claims were being made? PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Karic, please don't answer for the moment. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I object to this question. The Defence counsel is talking about a conclusion. The witness said he got information. PRESIDING OFFICER: Mr. Hodzic, can you perhaps rephrase that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the basis for this assessment, for this conclusion, on the basis of which -- PRESIDING OFFICER: I'm sorry. I don't think -- Mr. Withopf, can you perhaps explain in more -- what the nature of your objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I object to the word "conclusion" in the question. The witness, in his previous answer, had said he got information that members of the 9th and 10th Brigades committed the crimes. This is not a conclusion. I object to use the word "conclusion" in the Defence counsel questioning the witness. PRESIDING OFFICER: Right. We know -- sorry. Yes, Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the objection and I will respond to it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, and please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of the information?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was information obtained from Dzankovic that was forwarded to us on the 9th and on the following day, the morning, at around 11.00 in the morning, it was from Namik Dzankovic, an officer of the security department. He had such information we he obtained in the course of his work. And by personally visiting Donja Grabovica, the area where the crime had been perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know on the basis of what kind of information did he arrive at such a position?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We asked him the same question. Zicro Suljevic, Bilajac and myself asked him this question when we were informed of the matter. He said he found out about this through the security organ of the 44th Brigade in Jablanica and through the municipal organs of the Ministry of the Interior, which had an overthrough of the situation down there. And later through Dzankovic we formed an entire team which went to carry out a full investigation, which is what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to certain information, mention was also made of certain refugees and displaced persons, and they were also suspects. Are you aware of this at all?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question. PRESIDING OFFICER: Sorry. Again, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I object to this question. I refer to Rule 90(h)(i) and Rule 90(H)(ii).

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Thank you. PRESIDING OFFICER: Indeed. And just so Mr. Karic understands, basically, if I've understood it correctly, this is going beyond the subject-matter of the examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You understood completely correctly, and it hasn't been discussed yesterday, and the Prosecution understands that the requirements of Rule 90(H)(ii) are not met. PRESIDING OFFICER: Yes. I think this is an area we will just have to note for the Trial Chamber when looking at the deposition. Mr. Hodzic, how much further did you want to go down this route? My difficulty is that there is an objection that I cannot rule upon. Now, this poses the difficulty as to whether or not we should proceed. I think the best thing to do would be if you could move to another line of questioning for the moment, and I may see if I can get some immediate instruction from the Trial Chamber during the next break or so. So if I could ask you to move on to a different area for now, Mr. Hodzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, an interview was conducted with you prior to this hearing.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in December of last year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the interview, were you shown a transcript of the interview in the Bosnian language before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't shown a transcript of the interview, but the organs of investigation provided me with a copy of the cassettes. There were nine cassettes, which were numbered, and apart from the translation mistakes, especially the translation mistakes with regard to military terminology, I have no significant objections to make to that translation into the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this interview, did anyone offer you protective measures of any kind?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Protective measures in what sense?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Protective measures for a witness.

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the surgeons from the general hospital who operated on me wanted to establish whether I was in a position to fly to The Hague and to testify in The Hague. Their response was negative, because the operation was a serious one. It was an operation on my stomach. And they suggested that my hearing should be conducted in this manner. And this is what I requested. Because of the situation, I feel this is necessary today too. So these are the matters that were discussed, and this was taken into consideration. As you can see, I'm in Sarajevo now, and this is far more acceptable for me. It's better for me than if I had travelled to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you offered to be moved to some third country?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Presiding Officer, I have finished my cross-examination. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. Mr. Withopf, will you have some re-examination for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We have some re-examination, and it will be a very short one. PRESIDING OFFICER: Would you like to do that immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If possible, yes. I anticipate only five minutes. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you very much. Re-examined by Mr. Withopf:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, in respect to the interview, the statement that has been taken in December 2002, you were just mentioning translation mistakes, mistakes in respect to translation of military terms. What are these translation mistakes about?

utterances.speaker: VEHBIJA KARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listened to the cassettes and I came to the conclusion that they had not been -- it had not been translated professionally. But this does in no way affect the substance of my testimony. And it's very difficult to translate such terminology in such a short period of time, from Bosnian into English, and any professional terminology is problematic. It can be interpreted in various ways. But I didn't notice that the substance had in any way been affected by these minor translation mistakes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We have no further questions. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. Before we finally release the witness, I think there are a couple of small points in relation to documents. Mr. Karic, we have two documents that procedurally we have identified only. One is your diary, to which you've referred at times during your evidence. We have copies of that, and I do appreciate that it is your personal diary. But is there any possibility that we may be able to have the original of that diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the diary in front of me. I offered the diary to your representatives, and they photocopied it, from the 1st of June, 1993, for a six-month period. I thought that this period was sufficient. I didn't have any conditions. I placed it at their disposal and they took what they needed. They photocopied and they returned the original to me. But I intend to use this diary, if my health permits me to do so, in order to write a book on the war. I feel this is something that I owe myself and I owe my family. So this diary, the original one, such as it is, is essential to me. But I can provide your colleague, who is sitting by me, with this diary so that she can photocopy it. PRESIDING OFFICER: Well, thank you. We have, as you say, the photocopies of the relevant excerpts, but I think it would help us for the record if you could just tell us the time period covered by the entire volume that you have. Do you understand what I'm asking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand you fully. I'll tell you immediately. From the Monday, the 1st of March, 1993, and the last date is the 31st of December, 1993. So it's Monday, from Monday, the 1st of March, 1993, up until the 31st of December, 1993. That is the period that is covered. It's a nine-month period. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you, Mr. Karic. You keep your diary, and there is a very small possibility that at some stage someone would ask to come and have another look at the original. But if you could just keep it safely in your possession. The other matter is the order that came up earlier today, the one that you have a copy of in Sarajevo, and again, we just need to make sure that the court deputy takes a copy of that. You explained that what we have is indeed a copy, so a photocopy will be sufficient for us. Right. I believe that deals with any matters to do with documents. I would just like to discuss briefly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your colleague photocopied something during the break. I'm now looking at my copy and your copy. PRESIDING OFFICER: And are they the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Completely identical. PRESIDING OFFICER: Good. Thank you. There is just one point I would like to go over with counsel before formally releasing you, Mr. Karic, but I think it's probably better to do that not in front of you. If you would like to just take a short break for a couple of minutes or so, and the court deputy will then come and get you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Gentlemen, I just want to go back to the objection that was raised in relation to that question of the witness. The objection from the Prosecution was on the basis that the point had not been raised in examination-in-chief, and this was to do with a question put by Mr. Hodzic about reference to refugees and displaced persons being suspects. The objection from the Prosecution is on the basis of Rule 90(H) of the Rules, which does provide that examination -- cross-examination can go beyond the scope if it's a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. So in this situation, relevant for the defence case. That can only be done if the counsel, so Mr. Hodzic, can put to the witness the nature of the case, so that it is clear what is the contradiction in the evidence. Given the fact that there is a very little possibility that we would have the opportunity to go back to Mr. Karic in the future, I am concerned that if there is any issue here that should be put to him, that it is put to him today. But to do that, Mr. Hodzic would have to be able to set out the nature of the defence case. Now, I don't know, Mr. Hodzic, if you would like to respond to that or whether you'd like a few moments to think about how you would respond. And Mr. Withopf, I should give you the opportunity to say whether or not I've summed up the situation correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Ms. Featherstone, you certainly summed up the situation a hundred per cent correctly. Defence counsel request that to put to the witness the Defence case at least in respect to the question he was going to ask to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I was afraid of at the beginning, because I'm not familiar with the procedure and I wanted to avoid any errors. But the first information obtained after the crime had been perpetrated -- according to the first information, the perpetrators were not known, and it is within this context that I asked this question as to whether he knew anything about this. And later on it was stated that these were -- the perpetrators were members of the 9th and 10th Brigade. But we found out that this was established only later on, in October, the 26th of October. So there's a possibility of having other witnesses who will appear before the Tribunal and be able to testify with regard to this matter. So I don't think that I would go forward with this question. I don't know whether I have stated my position correctly in terms of the procedure, but if I haven't, I do apologise. I apologise because I -- from the very start, I haven't been assisted by co-counsel and I need co-counsel for the sake of procedure, in order to proceed in a correct manner. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. I think that clarifies the matter, that there's no need to question this witness further on that point, and I thank you for that assistance. Right. Then if we can speak to the court deputy in Sarajevo, if the witness could be brought back in, and I will release him. There's nothing further for the witness? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: PRESIDING OFFICER: Hello again, Mr. Karic. Thank you for that little break. I'm pleased to inform you that there will be no more questions for you. Thank you very much for coming and giving your evidence to the Tribunal in this fashion. The full transcript of this evidence, plus the videotapes, plus a report from myself as Presiding Officer, will go to the Trial Chamber that eventually hears this case. As I say, I thank you for this. You are released from your obligations and we wish you well. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Goodbye, and wish you all the best. PRESIDING OFFICER: Thank you. We're adjourned, then. I would just remind counsel that we have a Rule 65 ter meeting this afternoon at 3.00. Mr. Hodzic, it's an informal procedure. You do not need to wear your robes. And someone from the court deputy's office will bring you to the room where the meeting takes place. And we do have interpretation available. Thank you, everyone. We're adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.41 a.m.
